observability-fundamentals.r: A service was slow for some customers, but averages looked healthy. Breaking latency down by customer and endpoint in the metrics, then following one slow trace, showed a single tenant with a huge query.
observability-fundamentals.x: Observability is the ability to ask new questions without shipping new code. Collect high-quality, correlated signals, keep context such as request identifiers, and be honest about what you cannot see.

metrics-and-prometheus.r: A dashboard showed an average response time of 120 ms while some users waited over five seconds. A histogram and a high percentile revealed the slow tail that the average hid.
metrics-and-prometheus.x: Use histograms and percentiles, understand rate and counter resets, and watch label cardinality. Know the limits of a single Prometheus and when to federate or use long-term storage.

logs-and-traces.r: A request failed across five services and the logs from each looked fine. A trace with one shared identifier showed that the third service waited for a slow call to the fourth.
logs-and-traces.x: Logs tell you what, traces tell you where. Propagate context everywhere, sample deliberately so you keep errors and slow requests, and keep personal data out of both.

log-pipelines.r: A log pipeline fell behind during a traffic spike and dropped lines at the worst moment. Adding a buffer and backpressure meant logs arrived late but were not lost.
log-pipelines.x: A pipeline is a production system. Plan for bursts, buffering, parsing errors and cost, and choose between indexing everything and storing cheaply with label-based search.

opentelemetry.r: A company wanted to change observability vendors but had instrumented every service with a proprietary library. With a vendor-neutral standard, switching meant changing a collector setting, not rewriting code.
opentelemetry.x: A standard protects you from lock-in but does not remove the cost of good instrumentation. Use auto-instrumentation to start, add manual spans where business meaning lives and control sampling at the collector.

synthetic-and-blackbox-monitoring.r: All internal dashboards were green while customers in one region could not log in because of a DNS problem. A probe from outside, running the login journey, would have caught it first.
synthetic-and-blackbox-monitoring.x: Measure from the user's side. Probe from several locations, test real journeys, and treat probes as a source of truth that can disagree with internal metrics.

alerting-and-dashboards.r: An on-call engineer got two hundred alerts a night and began ignoring them. Alerting on user-visible symptoms with clear runbooks cut it to a handful a week, and every one was worth waking up for.
alerting-and-dashboards.x: Every page should be urgent, actionable and new. Alert on symptoms, route by ownership, group related alerts and review noisy ones every week. A dashboard answers a question; if nobody asks it, remove it.

red-use-and-golden-signals.r: A team tracked fifty metrics per service and still could not tell if it was healthy. Switching to rate, errors and duration for services and utilisation, saturation and errors for resources made health obvious.
red-use-and-golden-signals.x: Start with a small set of signals and add more only to answer a question. Be clear about the difference between a service and a resource view, and about what saturation means for each.

telemetry-cost-and-cardinality.r: A developer added a user identifier as a metric label, and the number of series grew by millions overnight, slowing queries and doubling the bill. Removing that label and moving the detail into logs fixed it.
telemetry-cost-and-cardinality.x: Cardinality and retention drive cost. Put high-cardinality data in logs or traces, review the largest series regularly and set budgets so teams see the cost of what they add.

structured-logging-and-log-design.r: Searching logs for a customer problem meant guessing at free-text formats. Structured fields with consistent names made the same search a single filter.
structured-logging-and-log-design.x: Log design is an API. Use consistent field names, levels and identifiers, keep secrets out and make each line useful alone. Decide what you will want at 3 a.m. and log that.

runbooks-and-dashboards-for-on-call.r: At 3 a.m. an engineer new to the service followed a runbook step by step and fixed the problem without waking anyone. The runbook had been tested in a drill the previous month.
runbooks-and-dashboards-for-on-call.x: A runbook that has not been run is a guess. Keep them short, linked from alerts, owned and tested, and automate the safe steps. Fix the cause that makes the alert fire.

debugging-with-telemetry.r: A rise in errors appeared on a dashboard. Metrics showed which endpoint, a trace showed which dependency was slow, and logs from that dependency showed a full connection pool. Three signals together told the story.
debugging-with-telemetry.x: Move from symptom to cause with a repeatable path. Form a hypothesis, check it against another signal, and note where telemetry was missing so you can add it afterwards.
